title: An Alternative to I/We/You
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane argues against treating I/we/you -- model, then guided practice, then independent practice -- as the default structure for an entire math lesson, proposing instead a 'gradual increase in difficulty' model where teacher support is adaptive rather than following a predetermined release schedule. Rather than one big jump from full support to full independence, Kane breaks a lesson into a sequence of small steps of varying difficulty (he sketches a concrete pattern like you/I/you/you/I/you, then I/we/you, then I/you/I/you, then you/you, then I/you), with students working independently far earlier and more often than a strict I/we/you lesson would allow. He grounds the case in several concrete classroom benefits: fewer catastrophic 'too big a jump' lessons that unravel during independent practice, more frequent opportunities to check understanding throughout the lesson rather than only at the end, easier interleaving of skills, room for non-routine problems earlier, and less total teacher explanation time because explanations arrive in small, well-prepared chunks. Kane is careful to note he isn't rejecting I/we/you outright -- he still uses it as one tool within the larger structure -- but rejects it as an organizing principle for a whole lesson.
points: Kane's central reframe is 'gradual release of responsibility' (I/we/you) versus 'gradual increase in difficulty' -- the latter varies support based on the actual difficulty of each small step rather than following a fixed one-way release schedule.

His concrete lesson pattern (you/I/you/you/I/you, then I/we/you, then I/you/I/you, then you/you, then I/you) shows students doing independent work far earlier and more frequently than a standard I/we/you lesson permits.

He identifies a specific, common failure mode of I/we/you lessons -- the jump in difficulty being too large, causing the 'I' and 'we' stages to drag on until there's no time left for independent practice -- and argues gradual increase in difficulty structurally avoids it.

Kane connects the approach to a reduction in total explaining time: because explanations happen in small, well-prepared chunks rather than covering an entire topic up front, 'that adds up to way less time explaining.'
He's explicit that I/we/you 'isn't totally broken' and remains one tool within his approach -- the critique targets using it as the structure for an entire lesson, not the technique itself.
quotes: I’m not a fan of I/we/you lessons. I/we/you is the default lesson structure for lots of math teachers. Start by modeling a skill. Then work through the skill as a class. Then give students some independent practice.
Instead of I/we/you with gradual release of responsibility, I think it‘s more helpful to think of a gradual increase in difficulty.
The stuff we want kids to learn doesn’t break down into nice neat steps that are all the same size.

I've seen -- and taught -- plenty of I/we/you lessons that are a bit of a mess. The jump in difficulty is just too big. The teacher knows it's a bit of a mess, so the "I" and "we" stages drag on. There's not much time left for independent practice, half the class is confused, and it all ends in a muddle.

I realize that the difference between a gradual release of responsibility and a gradual increase in difficulty may seem small. But I think it’s a really valuable paradigm shift, and it opens up a ton of opportunities that are lost in a typical I/we/you structure.
I/we/you isn't totally broken -- I use it as one element of the gradual increase approach. But it's just one strategy for me, rather than a way to structure an entire lesson.
